profile.name: Mandilatos
profile.tagline: A wedding couples' dance of Western Thrace led by waving handkerchiefs.
profile.insight: Danced during wedding processions in Western Thrace, the couples' Mandilatos derives its name from handkerchiefs waved by dancers while guests carry mirrors and brooms.
profile.profile: Mandilatos (also associated with Sygkathistos) is a traditional couples' dance from Western Thrace in Southeastern Europe. Performed primarily during wedding celebrations, it accompanies the festive procession as guests escort the bride or best man to the church. Dancers hold handkerchiefs (mandilia) while navigating the procession alongside guests carrying symbolic mirrors and brooms. A closely related arm-focused variant known as rachenitsa is performed in Northern Thrace.
profile.profile_long:
Origins and History
Mandilatos is a traditional wedding couples' dance originating from Western Thrace, a area situated within Southeastern Europe. Historically integrated into local matrimonial customs, the dance functions as a celebratory procession where wedding guests escort the bride or the best man to the church. Its name directly reflects its physical central motif, deriving from the handkerchiefs (mandilia) that dancers display and hold during the performance.

How It Is Danced
Executed as a couples' dance, Mandilatos features continuous open engagement between partners centered around handheld props. Rather than maintaining a closed partner frame, dancers hold and manipulate handkerchiefs throughout the movement. The dance steps progress dynamically along the wedding procession route, adapting to the forward movement of the escort party.

Music and Instruments
Traditional Thracian musical ensembles supply the swift, rhythmic accompaniment for Mandilatos. The high-pitched Thracian gaida (a regional bagpipe variant known historically as askaulos) serves as the leading melodic instrument, frequently complemented by clarinets and toumbelekis percussion. Regional musical traditions also record related melodic formats such as Mandilatos(Mandra) and Hijaz Mandilatos(Hicaz Mandra).

Costume and Setting
Mandilatos takes place outdoors along village pathways and church courtyards during wedding celebrations. The dancers wave mandilia (handkerchiefs) as essential movement props. During the escort procession, surrounding wedding guests carry ceremonial objects laden with traditional symbolism, including mirrors to represent the bride's purity and brooms to signify domestic care and housekeeping ability.

Occasions and Meaning
Mandilatos is intrinsically linked to matrimonial rituals in Western Thrace. Danced during the escort of the bridal party or the best man to the church, it serves as a public celebration of community bonds and life transitions. The accompanying ceremonial items—handkerchiefs, mirrors, and brooms—form an explicit symbolic vocabulary celebrating family life and ritual purity.

Notable Figures
While traditional village community members and bridal parties historically maintain the dance, regional folk musicians such as Vangelis Dimoudis and folklorist Domna Samiou have documented and preserved the broader Thracian musical repertoire that supports dances like Mandilatos.

Regional Variants
Within Western Thrace, Mandilatos is closely linked with Sygkathistos, another free-style couples' dance performed during bridal processions where scarves and gifts are exchanged. In Northern Thrace (Bulgaria), a structurally similar arm-focused couples' dance is known as rachenitsa (derived from 'raka', meaning arm).

Lineage
Mandilatos forms part of the broader pan-Thracian dance heritage that spans modern Greek, Bulgarian, and Turkish Thrace. It shares rhythmic and structural affinities with Eastern Thracian Mandra variants and Northern Thracian arm dances, reflecting interconnected Balkan folk traditions.

basic_steps: Hold handkerchief (mandilato) in hand while facing partner
Step forward with light running or walking steps along the procession line
Wave the handkerchief rhythmically in opposition or harmony with partner steps
